facts.claim: Introduction: Meadows perches a Slinky on one upturned palm, grasps it from the top with the other hand, pulls the bottom hand away; the lower end drops and yo-yos. Students say 'Your hand. You took away your hand.'

She repeats it with the box the Slinky came in: nothing happens, the box just hangs. The answer lies within the Slinky; the hands suppress or release behavior latent in the spring's structure. 'That is a central insight of systems theory.'

'The system, to a large extent, causes its own behavior!' An outside event may unleash it, but the same event on a different system likely gives a different result. Her examples: competitors rarely cause a company to lose market share; the losing company creates its losses at least in part through its own policies; the flu virus does not attack you, you set up the conditions.
Balancing loop example: a cup of hot coffee cools toward room temperature; rate depends on the difference; iced coffee warms. Thermostat-furnace keeps a room near its setting.

Reinforcing loop: amplifying, self-multiplying, snowballing, a vicious or virtuous circle. Examples: 'the more my brother pushed me, the more I pushed him back'; soil erosion fewer roots more erosion; 'the more I practice piano, the more pleasure I get ... the more I play'.
Bank account: the more money, the more interest, added back to earn more. Doubling time approx 70 divided by growth rate: $100 at 7% doubles in 10 years; at 5% in 14 years.

Meadows challenges students to name a decision made without a feedback loop; most common answers are falling in love and committing suicide. 'If you see feedback loops everywhere, you're already in danger of becoming a systems thinker!'

Car dealership: keeps inventory covering ten days of sales; three delays: perception (averages sales over five days), response (makes up one-third of a shortfall per order), delivery (five days from factory). A permanent 10 percent jump in sales causes oscillations: she orders too much, then too little.

'It isn't because the car dealer is stupid'; she lacks timely information and faces physical delays. Shortening perception delay to two days: oscillations a bit worse; shortening reaction to two days: very much worse. Increasing response delay from three days to six greatly damps them. 'High leverage, wrong direction.'
Meadows: try a shower with a very long pipe between mixer and showerhead to feel hot and cold oscillations from a long response delay.

Further examples in the Introduction: political leaders don't cause recessions or booms, ups and downs are inherent in the structure of the market economy. Definition: a system is a set of things interconnected so that they produce their own pattern of behavior over time. Also: oil-exporting nations are not solely responsible for oil-price rises; importing nations' consumption, pricing and investment policies built economies vulnerable to supply interruptions.

Social networks gain and lose users via reinforcing loops
